newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan steps up moves to attract foreign capital.
newsitem.headline: Jordan steps up moves to attract foreign capital.

text.p: Jordan's plan to scrap a limit on foreign ownership of publicly listed stocks will enhance its regional competitiveness in the race to attract emerging market funds, local analysts said on Tuesday.

Jordan's top investment body's decision to scrap a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling on most publicly listed stocks, expected to be approved by the cabinet on Tuesday, follows another groundbreaking move this week by the Central Bank which lifted restrictions on foreign currency transfers.

The two steps have far reaching implications in enhancing global investor confidence in Jordan, which has until recently been sidestepped by investors excited about its regional competitors such as Egypt, Morocco and Lebanon.

"We are now coming close to the level of neighbouring countries, Jordan has now qualified...to come back into the race to attract foreign capital," said Omar al-Masri, an investment analyst running Amman-based Atlas Investment Group dealing with emerging funds.
Now Jordan would be better able to compete in the scope of incentives it offers for global emerging market capital in both portfolio and long term direct investors, Masri said.
Wahib Shair, director of the Amman Financial Market, said: "There are now tangible steps which I believe will have the nature of a snowball effect and one move will encourage the other.
"We passed the turning point, we are at the begining of a new phase...in which Jordan's attractiveness for foreign investors is now beyond question," Shair added.
Shair predicted substantially higher capital inflows as foreign and local and confidence in the economy would reflect itself in the bourse and inject more liquidity.
Once approved by the cabinet, the measure allows banks, telecommunications, transport, and insurance to be fully foreign owned, analysts said.
This will rank Jordan as among the most open stock markets in the region, in line with Egypt, Morocco Turkey and Israel.
Deputy Prime Minister Jawad Anani, who heads the higher investment council which approved scrapping the ceiling, told Reuters the move was designed to help attract foreign investment to Jordan.
Three sectors - construction, general retail trade and mining - were excluded from the new ruling and will be left subject to future revision.
The mining sector includes the strategic potash and phophates industries which already have substantial Arab governmental holdings.
The removal of foreign ownership limits went far beyond investor expectations of a slight lifting to around 70 percent.
Jordan has been mulling the changes as part of efforts to attract investment, enabling the state to go ahead in wider state sell-off of its majority stakes in leading firms.

Investors expect the moves to bring new impetus to long delayed sales of the government's vast portfolio, covering an estimated 40 percent of the Amman Financial Market's capitalisation of 3.2 billion dinars ($4.5 billion).
The government is also serious about pushing forward with other economic legislation such as an intellectual property law and anti-monopoly laws to help boost investment.

Investors and officials alike say waiving the 50 percent ceiling should attract more global fund buying in the Amman Financial Market, until now hampered by lack of blue-chip stock, which already reached the previous foreign ownership ceiling.

"With this decision we hope there will be more attraction for foreign investments in all the sectors," Shair said, referring to the limited free float in companies such as Arab Bank and Jordan Islamic Bank, already exceeding the ceiling.
The first half of 1997 has seen bouts of unprecedented global buying of Jordanian stock prompted by attractive prices compared to regional competitors such as Egypt and Morocco. $1 = 0.709 dinars
